passage:
For most of last semester, Mohit told me I was the only person on campus who got him. "You're more of a brother than my own brother," he said once, after we'd talked until 3 a.m. about his parents' divorce. I felt proud to be that person.
Then in November I missed his call because I was at my cousin's engagement. By morning I had eleven messages: I was useless, fake, just like everyone else. I read them in the bathroom, shaking. My first instinct was to fire back something equally cruel. I didn't. I wrote, "I'm sorry I missed your call. I was at an engagement. I care about you, and I won't be spoken to like this. Let's talk when things are calmer."
He didn't reply for four days. Then: "Chai?" We're friends again, sort of. I, Divyansh, keep my phone on me now, but I don't pick up at 3 a.m. any more.

qa.q: How many messages had Mohit sent by morning?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel reading the messages in the bathroom, and why?
qa.a: Shaken and bewildered, because the friend who had called him more of a brother than a brother suddenly called him useless over one missed call.

qa.q: Which choice did Divyansh make instead of firing back, and why did it help?
qa.a: He apologised for the missed call, said he cared, and set a clear limit on how he would be spoken to, which kept the friendship possible without accepting the insults.

qa.q: What might Mohit have been feeling when the call went unanswered?
qa.a: Probably alone and panicky, perhaps fearing being abandoned, which made one missed call feel like proof that Divyansh didn't care.

grounding: A young man praised as the only one who understands his friend is suddenly called useless over a missed call, and answers with care and a steady boundary.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 12 February
Nilesh (19) came in today, confused and upset. For three months his roommate Tarun called him "the only one who understands me" and told others Nilesh was "basically perfect". Last week Nilesh couldn't lend Tarun his bike for a trip because he needed it to get to an exam. Since then Tarun has told the whole wing that Nilesh is selfish and "never cared". Nilesh said, "I don't know who I am to Tarun any more. A saint or a villain." He admitted he wanted to post something nasty back.
We talked about staying steady: being polite, keeping his own limits (like the bike), and not trading insults. We practised one sentence he could use: "I still care about you, and I won't argue about who I am."
Next step: follow-up next Thursday. I have also suggested Nilesh tell the warden if the wing gossip turns into harassment.

qa.q: Why couldn't Nilesh lend Tarun his bike?
qa.a: He needed it to get to an exam.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's line 'A saint or a villain' suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Bewildered and hurt, because he was treated as perfect one week and selfish the next, with no middle ground where he is just a person.

qa.q: Which choice from the counselling session is most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Practising a calm sentence that keeps care and a limit together, so Nilesh can stay steady without posting something nasty back.

qa.q: How might other students in the wing see Nilesh after the gossip?
qa.a: Some may believe he is selfish, which adds to his hurt, while those who know him may see the story is one-sided.

grounding: A counsellor notes how a student idealised by his roommate and then called selfish over a refused favour is helped to keep steady boundaries without retaliating.

passage:
Thursday night
Three weeks ago Kavitha hugged me in the canteen and said, "You're the only one in this whole college who actually listens." She sent me songs at midnight. She told her mother about me.
Tonight I missed her call because I was in the library with my phone on silent. When I called back twenty minutes later, she said, "Don't bother. You're like everyone else, useless when it matters." Then she hung up.
I sat on the library steps feeling dizzy. What did I do? Twenty minutes. I typed something mean back. Deleted it. Typed "I'm sorry" four times. Deleted that too, because I'm not actually sorry for studying.
In the end I sent: "I was in the library. I care about you. Call me tomorrow if you want to talk." Then I put my phone face down.
I'm not going to be her saint or her enemy. Just me.
Shalini

qa.q: Where was Shalini when Kavitha called?
qa.a: In the library, with the phone on silent.

qa.q: Why did Shalini delete both the mean message and the 'I'm sorry' messages?
qa.a: Shalini felt hurt and dizzy but didn't want to hit back, and wasn't truly sorry for studying, so neither message felt honest.

qa.q: What choice did Shalini finally make, and why is it a steady one?
qa.a: Sending a calm message that explained, showed care and left the next step to Kavitha, which kept Shalini's balance without reacting in kind.

qa.q: What might be going on for Kavitha when she says 'useless when it matters'?
qa.a: She may have needed Shalini badly at that moment, and the missed call felt like abandonment, flipping her from praise to anger.

grounding: A student praised as the only one who listens is suddenly called useless after a missed call, and replies calmly without matching the anger.

passage:
In Hoshangabad, Kamini, nineteen, spent the Diwali rush behind the counter of her father's sweet shop, weighing kaju katli until her arms ached. Her phone buzzed twice in her apron pocket. She couldn't answer; the queue went out the door.
For months Rajni, from her teacher-training college, had called Kamini "the only one in this whole town who understands me". The next morning at the bus stand, Rajni wouldn't look at her. "She's useless," Rajni told the other girls loudly. "Selfish. When I actually need someone, gone."
Kamini's face burned. She wanted to shout back that Rajni was being dramatic. She didn't. She walked over and said quietly, "I missed your call because I was at the shop. I'm sorry. I can't answer during shop hours, but I'm free after eight tonight if you want to talk."
Rajni turned away. Kamini got on the bus, hands still shaking, and didn't take back a word.

qa.q: Why couldn't Kamini answer Rajni's calls?
qa.a: She was behind the counter of her father's sweet shop in the Diwali rush, and the queue went out the door.

qa.q: How did Kamini feel at the bus stand, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt; her face burned, she wanted to shout back, and her hands were still shaking on the bus.

qa.q: Which choice by Kamini kept a steady boundary without reacting in kind?
qa.a: She didn't shout back but apologised for the missed call, explained she can't answer during shop hours, and offered a time after eight.

qa.q: Why might Rajni flip from "the only one who understands me" to "useless"?
qa.a: Rajni may have felt abandoned when she needed Kamini, and in that strong feeling couldn't hold the good months and one missed call together.

grounding: Illustrates a young woman idealised by a friend and then publicly called useless after a missed call, who feels bewildered but holds a calm boundary.

passage: Jomon, you look confused. Your friend was calling you his rock, and now he says you're useless? Come, your Sangeeta akka has seen this before. I lay awake making lists of everything I'd done for her. I wanted to shout back. But my warden told me something wise: "Don't become the villain she needs. Stay the same." So I did. I didn't argue. I didn't beg. I was polite and steady. After a month, Beena came back, embarrassed. I let her, but carefully.

"I was in the lab, phone in the locker. I called back at six."
"Six was too late. You're useless, Asif. Honestly, you're like everyone else."

passage:
I'm Vidya, and in second year Joseph decided I was his whole world. "You're the only person in this college who actually understands me," he'd say on our walks round the hostel ground. I liked that. It felt special.

Then one night in November I missed his call. I was asleep; it was one in the morning. Next day he texted: "Knew it. You're like the rest. Useless when it counts." He told our group I was fake. I was completely bewildered. What had changed in one missed call?

I was tempted to send a long, angry reply listing everything I'd done for him. I didn't. I wrote: "I'm sorry I was asleep. I care about you. I can't always be awake at 1 a.m., but I'm around in the day." Then I stuck to that, even when he sulked.

By January we were talking again, carefully. I kept my phone on silent at night.

qa.q: At what time did Vidya miss Joseph's call?
qa.a: Vidya missed the call at one in the morning.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel after Joseph's "useless" text?
qa.a: Vidya felt bewildered and hurt, unable to understand how one missed call changed everything.

qa.a: It apologised, showed care and set a clear limit without reacting in kind, and Vidya then held that boundary steadily.

Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block B, 22 August.

Dilnaz came to my office this evening, confused and teary. Until last week her roommate called her "the only one who understands me" and they did everything together. On Tuesday Dilnaz missed one call during her tuition shift. Since then the roommate has told others Dilnaz is "useless" and "fake", and moved her things to the far side of the room.

Dilnaz asked me, "What did I do?" I told her missing a call was not cruel. We talked about staying kind but steady: one calm message, no arguing in the corridor, no chasing, no trading insults. She wrote the message in my office: "I'm sorry I missed your call. I was at work. I'm here if you want to talk."

I will also check in with the roommate tomorrow, separately, to see how she is doing.

Ganga

qa.a: Dilnaz missed one call on Tuesday, during her tuition shift.

qa.a: Dilnaz felt confused and hurt, teary and asking what she had done wrong.

qa.a: One calm message, no arguing in the corridor, no chasing and no trading insults, keeping kindness and boundaries together.
